confederation.name: the Skein
confederation.why_the_name: a skein is a flight of wild geese in the air and a loose hank of yarn; the Hundred are both -- free-flying, and tied together only loosely, by lines that are always being cut and tied again
confederation.people: the Aloft (their own word; they call themselves 'skeinfolk' to outsiders); the floor calls them highfolk, balloon people or, rudely, 'cloudies'
confederation.they_call_the_floor: the floor, the Ground; floor people are 'groundfolk' or 'heavies'
confederation.seat: none: the Skein has no capital, no standing council and no flag; its law travels with the knot keepers
confederation.law: knot-law: custom kept by each island's knot keepers in knotted cords and in books, argued at lashings; the Five Knots are the only laws every island keeps
five_knots: the Weight Knot: no island may take on more than its lift; the weigher's word on weight is final
the Flame Knot: no open flame aloft (hydrogen); fire is the only crime punished by putting a person down to the floor for good
the Line Knot: a line shot across must be made fast; no island refuses a lashing from one in distress
the Ten Knot: no raft of more than ten islands (since the Great Tangle, VY 388)
the Three-Day Knot: a raft casts off at the end of the third day; no island may rule another
confederation.lashing: when two islands come within 3 km, bell-speech and doves go first; if both agree (they almost always do), line rocketeers fire cold rockets trailing messenger lines across, heavier lines and hawsers follow, and the winch hands haul the islands together over an hour or two until their dock faces are 26 m apart; then the bridges come down on the facing sides and the islands become a raft. More islands may join a raft till it holds ten
confederation.the_moot: the three days lashed are the Lashing: a market, a moot, a fair and a wedding season at once. The knot keepers hear disputes; factors trade; young people cross to court, marry and move; the dead are mourned together; news of the floor is traded by the plumbs
confederation.casting_off: at dusk on the third day the Casting Off: bridges up, every lashing line cut with a knife by the eldest of each island, and the islands drift apart on the wind. 'Three days lashed and then the knives.'
confederation.why_three_days: long enough to trade, settle disputes and marry; short enough that no island grows used to ruling another, that the raft's slower drift doesn't carry it into weather, and that the weight that crosses doesn't unbalance anyone
confederation.why_ten: the Great Tangle (VY 388): seventeen islands lashed for a jubilee were caught by a squall line; the raft twisted, lines parted, Higgledy's sister island Piggledy was torn loose, holed on Tumbledown's rim and fell into the North Sea (212 lost). Ten is what the lines and the winches hold in a squall
confederation.between_islands: kin: marriage across bridges means everyone has cousins on a dozen islands; clan feuds and alliances follow the kin
confederation.families: large: four or five children is usual aloft (children are 'ballast', a blessing), so the Skein is young and its weight books are always full
confederation.coming_down: routine since the Mooring Compact (VY 418): islands moor at the floor's flea markets every few weeks, and the Aloft ride the gondolas down to trade, shop and visit kin in their thousands; ground-weight is a joke, not a fear. About half of all island children grow up to settle on the floor (the Full Book, VY 486): the Lowliners
confederation.line_or_ground: the Line or the Ground: since the Full Book (VY 486) every family raises its children knowing about half will go down the line to settle on the floor; a youth's going-down is feasted like a wedding, with a knotted cord to carry and a lantern to hang in the new home

physics.eotvos_rule: an island running antispinward (west) at v m/s relative to the floor feels g x (1 - v/290)^2: at its 6 m/s drift ~0.887 g. Lift and weight both scale with g, so a lighter g does not by itself float anything; what the Aloft exploit is that the envelopes reach up 1 km into faster westerly air, which drags the whole island west faster than the air round its deck. Relative to the air it sits in, the island is running antispinward, so it weighs less against that air's buoyancy: about 2% (2 x 3 m/s / 290 m/s), which on a 30,000 t island is 600 t -- the weight of all its trade. They call it the Lightening.
physics.gas: hydrogen, made aboard by electrolysis of cloud water and snowmelt; skycloth loses about 0.3% of an envelope's gas a week (and air creeps in), ~3,400 m3 a day an envelope, ~15 MWh of electrolysis (4.5 kWh/m3)
physics.power: the sunskin: the Steward's envelopes were skinned in photovoltaic film; half an envelope's 314,000 m2 faces the Sunline at a time, and even aged to a few per cent efficiency it makes ~40 MWh a day -- enough for the gas, the winches and the island. The Aloft can patch sunskin but not make it: new envelopes of plain skycloth must be carried by the old, which is why an island's oldest envelope is its treasure; roofs add a little from rationed floor cells
physics.lift_per_block_t: balloons(N) x net lift / N: 1 block 3 envelopes (22,000 t of lift for ~10,500 t: small islands are buoyant and carry ballast water), 10 blocks 17 envelopes (~12,500 t a block: a 15% margin before the Lightening, and the ponds can be drained for 900 t more)
physics.foamed_stone: the rock is 'skystone': foamed glass-ceramic the Steward cast from the Spindle's slag, 120-250 kg/m3 (real foam glass is 100-300 kg/m3), a crust over a honeycomb of sealed cells; it looks like dark volcanic rock, floats on water, and moss roots in its pores
physics.cold: about 5 C colder than the floor at the deck (environmental lapse ~6.5 C/km), more in the wind; the envelopes' tops near 1.8 km are ~11 C colder
physics.snow: the Steward keeps the cloud interiors cold (since VY 212 it has made the floor's rain as snow aloft, melting on the way down -- the cold-rain process of real clouds); an island passing through a cloud is snowed on, and the snow lies till the sun and the dry air take it slowly
physics.water: fog and cloud nets (real fog collectors yield 3-10 L/m2/day in fog; inside a Columbia cloud the nets run for hours) and snowmelt

history.what: the Hundred: after the Last Snow (VY 212) the Steward launches a hundred cloud engines -- platforms of foamed stone under great cylindrical envelopes, each with a sealed Box -- to make the floor's rain as snow aloft. To the floor they are 'the weather hulks' for sixty years
the Third Lockdown and the Regression; in the Gray Years people look up at the hulks, which the Steward still lowers to the Mooring Fields every few years for its tenders

the First Boarding: forty-one families of dissolved Warden lines, who knew the hulks' service routine, climb the tethers of a hulk moored near Bellhaven and refuse to come down. The Steward, bound not to cause death, raises the hulk to its height with them aboard and stops servicing it -- it leaves its Box running and lets the people keep the rest. The hulk is named Halyard
the Boardings: Gray Years families, Returner remnants after the Reconciliation (VY 280), debtors, dreamers and Waymakers take hulk after hulk at the Mooring Fields; each boarding group becomes a clan
the Mooring Fields close: the Steward stops lowering the hulks; from now on the only way up is a line
the First Lashing: Halyard and Bowline lash with ropes fired from spring guns; the three-day custom begins (the first lashing broke on the fourth day in a quarrel over water)
the Lockout: the Floor is set; the Aloft lose little (they had little) and gain trade: the floor now needs what they make
the Hundredth Boarding: the last hulk (Ragamuffin) is taken, by children of other islands sent to found it
the Skein named at a raft of nine; the Five Knots set down by the knot keepers
the Great Tangle: seventeen islands lashed for a jubilee meet a squall line; Piggledy falls into the North Sea with 212 aboard. The Ten Knot
the Gift of the Air: the Chutes release the floor's first aerostats; the Aloft trade for them within a year and strip them for parts

the first lark: Topgallant's wrights build a two-person aerostat from Gift parts, skycloth and a winch motor that climbs from the floor to an island in four minutes; the plumbs stop riding containers down the hoist lines

the Mooring Compact: Harrow Falls and the Skein's factors agree that every town keeps a mooring ground beside its weekend flea market -- anchor blocks, masts and, in the cities, whole Mooring Fields (the old name, from the hulks' service days) -- and the islands moor there to trade by gondola; Traders' Landing is the first
the first passenger gondolas: Andean-style jig-back cabins on track ropes from the islands' rims, crewed by the new Lines; within a decade every island keeps a mooring crew of twenty-four
the air post: Fathom and Dogwatch start carrying urgent letters for the floor by lark

the first Line Rows: island-born settlers fill the old cannery streets behind Solana Point's harbour and build up and over them in their islands' styles; the South Shore becomes the Lowliners' heartland
the Lark Quarrel: the Aerostat Pilots' Guild tries to bar larks from the Kettle Cup; the Aloft win three of the next five

the Settlers' Shares Act: island-born settlers receive a birth share after two years' registration (the floor-born get theirs at 18); until then the Registry had refused them shares, and settler couples borrowed shares to marry -- a wound still felt

the Full Book: the islands' weight books fill as the Skein's numbers peak; at a raft of ten the knot keepers agree that no island will carry more than its lift, and that each family's children choose the Line or the Ground. Since then about half go down, some 1,500 a year

the Draw Housing Ruling: after a hard summer of disputes in Solana Point and Oceanview, the Assembly rules that settlers queue for Draw homes like everyone else; the South Shore's poorer streets resent it, the Line Halls call it fair
the Launch Day Notice (VOYAGE ONE THIRD COMPLETE) reaches the Skein by dove in two days; the knot keepers call a raft to talk of it

physiology: born and raised at about 0.89 g (0.925 g at the deck, less drifting west): taller by ~3 cm on average, lighter-boned and longer-limbed than the floor's (low-gravity bone and muscle unloading, over 8-9 generations of slight selection and every childhood at 89% weight -- modest, but visible in a crowd)
ground-weight: on the floor they feel 12% heavier; a day's walking leaves them sore, and the young get ground-sickness (dizziness, heavy limbs, homesickness) in the first days
cold-adapted habits rather than bodies: layered clothes, hot food, short exposure; frostnip on ears and fingers is common and treated without fuss
a head for heights: vertigo is taught out of children on the rim rails; floor people's fear of the edge amuses them
thin skin for flame: they have almost never seen open fire; candles on the floor fascinate and frighten them
water: the ponds and lakes are the island's reservoir and its ballast at once: filled by the cloud nets and snowmelt, drained by the weighers to trim (a 1,000 m2 pond a metre deep is 1,000 t of trim). Lined with skycloth over the foamed stone; reeds, frogs and stocked fish; they freeze over in a long white and are skated on. Every island has at least one pond; islands of six blocks or more have a small lake

goat.name: dwarf goat
goat.why: milk, cheese, meat, hair; light, sure-footed, eats anything

sheep.name: sheep (small hill breed)
sheep.model: small, dense fleece; only on rolling islands as a flock

duck.name: duck
duck.why: eggs, down, pest control in the gardens

goose.name: goose
goose.why: down (the down trade), watch-birds that shout at strangers

rabbit.name: rabbit
rabbit.why: meat, fur-felt, compost manure; no flight risk
rabbit.model: in hutches; a few loose ones are a scandal

dove.name: dove (pigeon)
dove.why: messages, eggs, meat on some islands, down

pig.name: pig (small)
pig.why: meat, eats scraps; heavy, so only where the lift allows

fish.name: pond fish: perch and pumpkinseed sunfish, crayfish

swallow.name: barn swallow
swallow.where: mud nests under the rim and on the rock's underside
swallow.what: hunts insects round the island; the islanders' luck-bird

swift.name: swift
swift.what: screaming flocks at dusk; never lands

sparrow.name: house sparrow
sparrow.what: came up in the first boardings' baggage

gull.name: gull
gull.where: follows islands over the seas, nests on the rim of a few
gull.what: a thief at the long kitchen

tern.name: tern
tern.where: rides with islands over the North and South Seas
tern.what: dives into the ponds for fish

wren.name: wren
wren.where: the moss and vines under the rim
wren.what: lives its whole life in the hanging gardens

heron.name: heron
heron.where: the lakes of great islands, visiting
heron.what: flies up from the floor's marshes to fish the lakes; an omen

frog.name: frog
frog.what: came up as spawn in hoisted water; sings at night

ballooning_spider.name: ballooning spider
ballooning_spider.where: everywhere; arrives on silk threads in the wind
ballooning_spider.what: real: spiders sail on silk; their threads glitter on the fences after a white

snail.name: snail
snail.what: a pest; the ducks eat them

cat.name: cat
cat.what: the mousers; sleep on the warm electrolysis halls

lichen_moth.name: lichen moth
lichen_moth.what: grey moths that live only aloft (a Columbia variety)

lark.name: the lark
lark.seats: tandem: the plumb forward, the second (navigator, trade clerk) behind
lark.how: a slim 14 m hydrogen envelope (a cigar, not a ball) over a light keel; four ducted fans on tilting pylons; a winch motor for the mooring line; low weight and a hard trim let it out-climb and out-run any floor aerostat (the floor's top out near 90 km/h)
lark.mooring: larks sit in cradles on the island's tallest roofs; a lark docks by flying up a dropped line
lark.per_island: at least two: one for the plumb, one spare and for rescue; great islands keep more

plumb.name: the plumb
plumb.why: a plumb line drops straight down
plumb.who: one chosen from the clan, usually for seven years: a trader, a diplomat and a pilot; with a second who flies behind and learns
plumb.does: goes down by lark to trade at the floor's markets and the Chutes, books the hoist schedule, carries letters and news, buys what the factors ask for, and brings back stories; the plumb still speaks for the clan, but since the moorings most Aloft meet groundfolk at the markets themselves
plumb.how_seen_aloft: honoured and a little pitied: the plumb carries the ground-weight for everyone
plumb.how_seen_below: glamorous, aloof, cold-handed; floor children chase their larks

hoist_trade.what: scheduled trade by hoist: the island trims to pass over an agreed spot (the floor's 'hoist grounds' at Drops, Chutes and market towns) at an agreed hour; the hoist masters drop long lines -- 750 m and more -- and the floor's dock hands hook on cargo containers; the winches draw them up. Down go the island's goods in the same containers
hoist_trade.container: the skybox: a light aluminium-framed container, about 2.4 x 2.4 x 3 m, at most 2 t loaded (the hoist lines' limit)
hoist_trade.schedule: booked by the plumb a week or more ahead; the weather reader picks the drift; an island makes a hoist every few days
hoist_trade.weight: every hoist is weighed both ways: what comes up must be balanced by what goes down, or by gas

market_moorings.what: the market moorings: every town on the floor keeps a mooring ground beside its weekend flea market; an island trims to arrive, descends to about 600 m, drops its mooring crew of 24 in a free-hanging drop cage, makes fast its hawsers to the anchor blocks or masts, raises logistics tents (the Mooring Office, the Weigh House, the Crew Tent) and then runs gondolas: passenger cabins of 28 with a cabin warden, and cargo cabins carrying skyboxes
market_moorings.how_often: a city sees an island about two weekends in five, a small town less often; islands drawn to a moored island lash on and drop their own lines; at three moored islands the market becomes a fair and the islanders' trading tents ring the parking lot
market_moorings.stay: most islands stay one weekend, some two or three; none more than three weeks. The Three-Day Knot is kept by the market knot: the lashings are renewed at a short moot every third day
market_moorings.anchors: cities keep Mooring Fields of buried anchor blocks and two mooring masts; towns a mast and an anchor ring; villages an anchor ring. Only the first islands make fast to the ground (six at a city, four at a town, three at a village); the rest lash to them as a raft, up to the Ten Knot's ten
market_moorings.bright_week: Bright Week: when five or more islands moor at one market it is a celebration, and the whole market -- the town's own booths too -- stays open every day while they stay. Customs: every island strings its lights across the whole market and lot (the brightest week of the town's year); the islands' bells ring the market open each morning; a lantern market runs in the aisles every evening; on the first night the Lines dance the rope-dance on the anchor field; floor children are given a first knot on a cord
market_moorings.sky_holiday: the Sky Holiday (the Aloft say 'the Low Sky', for a sky hung low with islands): when seven or more islands moor at a town's or village's market, the town council declares a holiday for the town and every place within eight kilometres. Work stops but for the essential trades; schools close; every house hangs a lantern; the islands bring the long kitchen down to the market field and the whole district eats together; children ride the gondolas free; the town band and the island bells play in turn. It lasts while seven stay, three days at most -- the Three-Day Knot again. Most towns see one in a lifetime, and date things by it
market_moorings.weather: islands moor only in light air; in a storm the gondolas stop and the island rides out on its hawsers, or casts off
market_moorings.weight: every person and load is weighed down and up at the Weigh House; the island takes on water ballast as its people go down
market_moorings.the_lines: the mooring crews (the Lines) are the most honoured trade aloft, paid in shares of the line toll (a fifth of every fare and freight fee)

line_ranks.name: the Mooring
line_ranks.what: commands the mooring: booking, approach, anchoring, the strike; sits with the Helm at lashings

line_ranks.name: anchor master
line_ranks.what: the hawsers, the anchor blocks and the three-day load survey

line_ranks.name: sheave keeper
line_ranks.what: the stations' bull wheels, drives and brakes; the daily inspection run

line_ranks.name: rope reader
line_ranks.what: walks and reads every rope and keeps the rope log

line_ranks.name: cabin warden
line_ranks.what: rides every passenger cabin: fares, safety and the visitors

line_ranks.name: line hand
line_ranks.what: shackling, rigging the tents, cargo and rescue on the rope

line_ranks.name: greenline
line_ranks.what: an apprentice of up to three years: knots, rope lore, the weigh book

settled.name: Lowliners: island-born settlers on the floor and their floor-born children who keep the identity (their own word, said with pride). [ETHNONYM placeholders: the floor's formal census term and the other peoples' proper names wait for the political work]
settled.by_region_note: most settle on the South Sea shore (a quarter of Solana Point is Lowliner); they are found everywhere, fewest on the North Sea shore
settled.why_south: chain migration to the first Line Rows (VY 452), the canneries' and harbours' work, the South Shore's open weekend markets, and the island routes, which moor most often at the Starlite Swap
settled.neighbourhoods: Line Rows: in the South Sea cities whole blocks are rebuilt as warrens in a hodge-podge of every island's style -- the city turns into warrens for blocks at a time; smaller Line Rows elsewhere; a Line Hall (guild, savings club, chapel, dance floor) in every city

regional_feeling.north: few and liked: neighbours, craftspeople and riggers; prejudice is hardly felt
regional_feeling.south: many, and real friction in the poorer streets: Draw housing queues, entry work at the canneries, docks and building sites, crowded schools, the lights and music late; warmer in the affluent districts and among those who work beside them

settled.trades: market trading, the ropeways' ground ends, building at height, rigging, lighting and sign work (the islanders' love of lights became a trade), knitwear, rope, bells and music, cooking; and every other trade, as any people
settled.institutions: the Line Halls; the Low Lashing, a reunion fair at Traders' Landing every June when as many islands as can moor at once; their own knot keepers for disputes
settled.the_other_way: surface people seldom settle aloft -- it takes a moot's consent, a place in the weight book and usually a marriage or a needed trade -- but it is not unheard of: perhaps fifty a year

rigger.name: rigger
rigger.what: climbs the tethers and the envelope nets; inspects, splices and trims the rigging
rigger.why: the envelopes are the island's life; every line is walked weekly

envelope_wright.name: envelope wright
envelope_wright.what: cuts, seams and patches skycloth; builds new envelopes over years
envelope_wright.why: skycloth leaks and wears; an envelope lasts about 40 years

gas_maker.name: gas maker
gas_maker.what: runs the electrolysis halls that split cloud water into hydrogen; keeps the gas books
gas_maker.why: the envelopes lose about 1% of their gas a week

winch_hand.name: winch hand
winch_hand.what: runs the winches and capstans: hoists, lashings, the bridges
winch_hand.why: everything that comes aboard comes up a line

line_rocketeer.name: line rocketeer
line_rocketeer.what: fires the cold (compressed-gas) line rockets that carry the first messenger lines across to another island
line_rocketeer.why: lashing begins with a 3 km shot

net_keeper.name: net keeper
net_keeper.what: tends the cloud nets and snow troughs that are the island's water, and the cisterns

roof_grower.name: roof grower
roof_grower.what: farms the roofs: greens, beans, berries, herbs, rooftop grain in boxes
roof_grower.why: every roof is a garden; every kilo of food grown aloft is a kilo not hoisted

beekeeper.name: beekeeper
beekeeper.what: keeps the cold-hardy bees of the roof gardens; honey and wax
beekeeper.why: bees are the gardens' pollinators aloft

dove_keeper.name: dove keeper
dove_keeper.what: keeps pigeons and doves: eggs, meat, down, and messages between islands
dove_keeper.why: birds carry word across the gap before the rockets fly

moss_grower.name: moss gatherer
moss_grower.what: harvests the underside's moss and vines from cradles slung under the rim: dye, medicine, packing, bedding
moss_grower.why: the underside garden is the only wild place aloft

snow_hand.name: snow hand
snow_hand.what: clears roofs and paths of snow after a cloud, packs it into the cisterns and the ice houses
snow_hand.why: a deep fall weighs hundreds of tonnes

weigher.name: weigher
weigher.what: keeps the island's weight book: every load hoisted or dropped, every birth and death; trims ballast
weigher.why: weight is the first law aloft

cook.name: cook
cook.what: cooks in the long kitchens; electric only -- no flame under hydrogen

healer.name: healer
healer.what: treats the sick and injured: falls, frost, line burns, ground-sickness
healer.why: the floor's hospitals are a day away

teacher.name: teacher
teacher.what: teaches the children: reading, figures, knots, weather, the weight book
teacher.why: children are the island's future weight

child_minder.name: child minder
child_minder.what: runs the crèche rooms while parents work the lines
child_minder.why: the lines are no place for small children

mender.name: mender
mender.what: carpenter and fixer: light framing, panels, stairs, roofs, fences
mender.why: everything aloft is light, so everything needs mending

sparks.name: sparks
sparks.what: the electricians: Sunline collectors on the roofs, cells, the Thirty-Two boards that run the winches and books
sparks.why: power is light caught on the roofs

smith.name: smith
smith.what: light-metal work: aluminium and titanium from the floor, cold-worked and riveted (no forges)
smith.why: a forge's flame is forbidden aloft

roper.name: roper
roper.what: spins and lays cordage: tethers, lashing hawsers, nets
roper.why: the Skein is tied together with rope

weaver.name: weaver
weaver.what: weaves skycloth for envelopes, and wool and down cloth for clothes
weaver.why: the Aloft dress warm and trade their cloth

knitter.name: knitter
knitter.what: knits the island's colours: hats, mittens, ganseys, leggings
knitter.why: the cold is constant; the patterns say who you are

tailor.name: tailor
tailor.what: cuts coats and the quilted down jackets
tailor.why: a coat aloft is a life

bridgewright.name: bridgewright
bridgewright.what: keeps the island's bridges; rigs the bridges at a lashing
bridgewright.why: the bridges are each island's pride and style

fence_warden.name: fence warden
fence_warden.what: walks the rim fences; rescue on the edge and in the nets
fence_warden.why: a fall from the rim is 750 m

hoist_master.name: hoist master
hoist_master.what: runs the scheduled cargo drops: lines down, containers up, the floor-side manifest
hoist_master.why: trade hangs on the hoist schedule

factor.name: factor
factor.what: trader: buys and sells for the island, at lashings and by hoist; keeps the clan's accounts

plumb.name: plumb
plumb.what: the clan's descender: flies the lark to the floor to trade, bargain and bring word back; one chosen at a time, with a second

lark_wright.name: lark wright
lark_wright.what: builds and keeps the larks (the clan's high-performance aerostats) and their mooring cradles

weather_reader.name: weather reader
weather_reader.what: reads the clouds, fronts and winds; plans the island's trim; sells forecasts to the floor
weather_reader.why: the island goes where the wind goes; the reader says where that is

knot_keeper.name: knot keeper
knot_keeper.what: keeps the island's law and records in knotted cords and books; arbitrates at lashings
knot_keeper.why: the Skein has no courts; it has knot keepers

box_tender.name: box tender
box_tender.what: watches over the Steward's Box (the sealed cloud engine on the island's mast) and keeps people from it
box_tender.why: the Box is the bargain the Hundred live by

brewer.name: brewer
brewer.what: brews the cold beers, meads and berry wines

musician.name: musician
musician.what: bell-ringer, singer, fiddler: bell-speech across the gap; the lashing dances

cleaner.name: compost hand
cleaner.what: keeps the compost works and the water closets: nothing is wasted or dropped
cleaner.why: every gram of soil was hoisted

shopkeeper.name: shopkeeper
shopkeeper.what: keeps the island's stores and stalls

herder.name: herder
herder.what: keeps the goats and sheep on the hill pastures and roof paddocks; milking, shearing, slaughter
herder.why: milk, wool and meat that never had to be hoisted

poultry_keeper.name: poultry keeper
poultry_keeper.what: keeps hens, ducks, geese and rabbits in the roof coops and the pond margins
poultry_keeper.why: eggs every day, feathers for the down trade

pond_keeper.name: pond keeper
pond_keeper.what: keeps the ponds and lakes: water level (the island's ballast), the fish, the reeds, the ice in winter
pond_keeper.why: the ponds are reservoir, ballast, fishery and the island's commons at once

elder_counsel.name: counsel
elder_counsel.what: elders who sit on the island's council and teach the young the lines

weather.name: weather readers
trade: forecasts for farms and the Aerostat Guild

ice.name: ice cutters
trade: snow and ice (a wonder on the floor since the Last Snow)

larks.name: lark wrights
trade: fans and envelopes for the Aerostat Guild

survey.name: map makers
trade: aerial surveys and maps of the floor

courier.name: air-post carriers
trade: air post: urgent letters and parcels by lark and dove

gas.name: gas makers
trade: hydrogen in bottles for other islands

trade.name: factors and brokers
trade: brokerage between islands and the floor

governance.helm: the Helm: a captain chosen for a year by every adult, who steers the trim and speaks at lashings
governance.council_elders: a council of elders (the Old Lines) by seniority on the ropes
governance.lot: a council drawn by lot every season from all over sixteen (sortition)
governance.mother_house: the mother house: the eldest woman of each line sits; descent and homes pass through mothers
governance.guild: the work-crews govern: riggers, gas makers, growers and factors each send a voice
governance.consensus: the whole island in the long kitchen until all agree (it can take days)
governance.plumb_rule: the plumb and the weigher jointly: the trading houses run the island

customs.cord_names: each child is given a knotted cord at birth; a knot is added for every lashing they cross a bridge at
customs.bell_speech: bell-speech: islands talk across the gap in rung patterns before the lines are shot

clothing.principle: warm, layered, light (every gram counts), knitted in the clan's colours so a stranger's island can be read at a glance; wind-proof shells over wool and down. names.convention: a given name, the clan (a founding surname, kept by all born to the clan) and the island: 'Wren Okafor of Halyard'.
